title: Latent profiles of parental discipline in Singapore: Intergenerational patterns and links to adjustment in young adulthood
content:
by Hoi Shan Cheung, Elinor Lim, Kelly M. Y. Chan, Charlene S. L. Fu, Clarissa Choo

Using a person-centered approach, this paper examined parental discipline profiles in Singapore from parents’ and young adults’ perspectives, and how these were linked to young adults’ adjustment. Two quantitative studies were conducted to explore parents’ experiences of disciplining their children (Study 1) and young adults’ experiences of receiving discipline (Study 2). Study 1 utilized the self-reported ISPCAN Child Abuse Screening Tool for Parents (ICAST-P) to document the frequency of use of 36 discipline methods. The ICAST-P was reworded for Study 2 to assess young adults’ experiences of being disciplined. Latent class analysis identified three groups of disciplinarians in each study. Study 1 (N = 747 parents; 80.7% mothers) showed that 14.6% of participants were harsh disciplinarians (high psychological-physical/violent discipline), 54.5% were high psychological-low physical/violent disciplinarians, and 30.8% were low psychological-physical/violent disciplinarians. Parents who endorsed physical discipline and had been physically punished during childhood were more likely to be harsh disciplinarians. Study 2 (N = 667; 74.3% females; age 18–25) showed three similar groups: harsh disciplinarians (4.0% mothers; 6.1% fathers), the high psychological-moderate physical/violent discipline group (34.0% mothers; 37.7% fathers), and the moderate psychological-low physical/violent discipline group (62.0% mothers; 56.1% fathers). Young adults whose parents used moderate psychological and low levels of physical/violent discipline had the least emotion dysregulation, the best parent-child relationship, and the highest self-esteem. The potential long-term impact of harsh discipline and intergenerational transmission of harsh discipline are discussed.
